prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "Datadog, Inc." (ticker DDOG). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)

   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))

   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)

   "nash": Tom Nash: the 12-step research process (“How to Find the Best Stocks in the Market” (Tom Nash, 2026))
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Datadog fits Gardner's Rule Breaker profile well: it leads cloud observability, is still run by co-founder Olivier Pomel, rose 79% over the 52 weeks to October 26, 2026, and is often called expensive at about 25 times sales. Its main gap is that it improved an existing category (monitoring) rather than creating a wholly new one.
summaries.buffett: Datadog has a sticky product with 80% gross margins and $915M of 2025 free cash flow, but GAAP operating income was negative ($-44M) in 2025, stock pay was $751M, and the shares trade at about 571 times trailing earnings. That puts it far outside Buffett's requirement of consistent owner earnings bought at a sensible price.
summaries.munger: Munger would respect the switching costs and founder-led culture, but would worry about the many paths to disappointment: cloud providers bundling cheaper tools, open-source OpenTelemetry, customer cost optimisation and a valuation that leaves little room for error. It is a high-quality business at a price he would likely call too rich.
summaries.lynch: Datadog is a clear Lynch fast grower, with revenue up 36% to $1.12B in Q2 2026, but Lynch warned against paying P/Es far above growth, and its forward P/E of about 111 on 2026 consensus EPS of $2.53 is several times its earnings growth rate. The story is simple to state but the price already reflects it.
summaries.fisher: Datadog fits Fisher's growth checklist closely: it has expanded from one product to 24 on a single platform, spends heavily on R&D ($1,548M in 2025, about 45% of revenue) with visible results, and sells efficiently through land-and-expand. Weaknesses on his list are thin GAAP margins and heavy stock-based dilution.
summaries.graham: Datadog fails nearly every Graham defensive test: it lost money in 2020-2022, has never paid a dividend, has only been public since 2019, and trades at about 571 times trailing earnings and 23 times book. It is financially strong, with about $5.0B of cash and securities against $986M of convertible notes, but there is no margin of safety on his terms.
summaries.thiel: Datadog partly fits Thiel's questions: it started by dominating cloud-native monitoring for DevOps teams and expanded into logs, APM and security, and its founders still run it. But it competes in a crowded market with Dynatrace, Grafana, Splunk and the cloud providers, so it is a leader rather than a monopoly with 10x better technology.
summaries.gerstner: Datadog matches Gerstner's interest in durable software growth tied to AI and cloud, with revenue growth re-accelerating to 36% and free-cash-flow margins near 30%. Its 'Rule of 40' score is well above 60, though at about 25 times sales the valuation already prices in years of strong execution.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller-style signals are positive: earnings and estimates are rising (2026 EPS consensus up from $2.42 to $2.53 over 90 days), revenue growth accelerated and the stock is in a strong uptrend. The main risks are a shift in liquidity or a slowdown in AI-native customers' spending, which would hit a high-multiple stock hard.
summaries.smith: Datadog meets Terry Smith's quality hurdles on gross margin (about 80%), cash generation and reinvestment runway, but fails on GAAP returns on capital (ROIC about 2.9%) once stock pay is counted. 'Don't overpay' is the clear problem at a 1.2% free-cash-flow yield.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Datadog ranks very poorly: its trailing GAAP operating income is close to zero (about $16M), giving an earnings yield near 0% on an enterprise value of about $97B. Its return on capital is similarly low on GAAP numbers.
summaries.akre: Akre's three legs partly line up: founder-led management with a long record, and a long reinvestment runway in observability, security and AI monitoring. The weak leg is the business's measured return on capital, which is low on GAAP figures because stock-based pay absorbs most operating profit.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for simple businesses in temporary trouble bought far below value with limited downside, and Datadog is a fast-growing, richly valued stock near its 52-week highs. Its net cash cushions the business, but the share price could still fall sharply, as it did by 68% from 2021 to 2023.
summaries.wood: Datadog fits ARK's view of AI and cloud software as an enabling layer, with LLM observability and Bits AI agents for operations, but it is not itself one of ARK's core platforms or a cost-curve story. Its addressable market grows steadily rather than many-fold in five years.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favours simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-rich businesses with high barriers to entry bought at a discount, and Datadog has the cash flow and stickiness but trades at about 85 times free cash flow. Its usage-based revenue also proved cyclical when customers optimised cloud spend in 2023.
summaries.sleep: Sleep's scale-economies-shared model fits only partly: Datadog reinvests heavily and gains scale, but customers often complain its usage-based bills are expensive rather than seeing savings passed back. Its founder-led, long-term culture matches his preferences better than its pricing approach does.
summaries.valentine: Datadog fits what Sequoia-style investors such as Valentine sought: a large, painful problem (keeping complex cloud systems running), technical founders and a market growing with cloud and AI. Today it is a $100B public company rather than an early-stage bet.
summaries.nash: Datadog does well on many of Nash's steps, including a real AI and cloud infrastructure trend, net cash, 36% revenue growth, a Rule-of-40 score above 60, a 90-point scorecard and steady earnings beats. It fails his instant-kill rule because its GAAP operating margin is under 1%, and his DCF values it well below $280.24.

momentum.evidence: DDOG rose 79.1% over the 52 weeks to October 26, 2026 (close $280.24), far ahead of the S&P 500's roughly 15% gain over the year to mid-October 2026.

g4.evidence: It is still run by co-founders Olivier Pomel (CEO) and Alexis Le-Quoc (CTO) since 2010, and institutions own about 87% of shares, but no single famous strategic backer stands out today.

g6.evidence: At about 25 times sales and 571 times trailing earnings it is often called expensive, though most analysts rate it Buy with an average target of $293.71.

simple.evidence: It is an established subscription software business, but observability, APM and security products are technical for a generalist.

b2.evidence: Revenue grew every year from $603M in 2020 to $3,427M in 2025, but GAAP results swung between losses (2020-2022) and small profits (2023-2025).

integrity.evidence: The founders have led openly for 16 years and the balance sheet is conservative, but stock-based compensation of $751M in 2025 (22% of revenue) and a dual-class share structure dilute and limit owners.

b6.evidence: It grows mainly by building its own products (from one to 24 on one platform) and makes only small tuck-in acquisitions (goodwill $531M at end-2025).

roic.evidence: GAAP ROIC is about 2.9% and ROE about 4.7% because stock-based pay absorbs most operating profit, though it uses no meaningful leverage.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow was $915M in 2025 versus net income of $108M, though much of the gap is $751M of non-cash stock compensation.

b10.evidence: Reinvestment grew revenue from $1,029M in 2021 to $3,427M in 2025, but the share price rose only about 66% over five years to October 2026 while diluted shares grew from 309M to 371M.

safety.evidence: At $280.24 it trades at about 85 times free cash flow and a Nash-style DCF gives roughly $85-105 per share.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 111 on 2026 EPS of $2.53 and about 94 on 2027 EPS of $2.98 is high even for 30% revenue growth.

mu5.evidence: Net cash and high retention limit failure risk, but bundled cloud-provider tools, open-source OpenTelemetry, customer cost cutting and concentration in AI-native customers are real threats.

reinvest.evidence: It keeps adding products such as security, LLM observability and Bits AI agents, with consensus revenue rising to $6,781M by 2028.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear fast grower: revenue rose 36% to $1.12B in Q2 2026 and is guided to $4.45-4.47B for 2026.

ly3.evidence: The forward P/E of about 111 is several times its expected EPS growth (about 18% from $2.53 in 2026 to $2.98 in 2027).

runway.evidence: Consensus sees revenue growing from $3,427M in 2025 to $6,781M in 2028 and about $9.4B in 2030 as it expands into security and AI monitoring.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares rose from 300M in 2020 to 371M in Q2 2026, and CEO Pomel sold about 127,000 shares for $32.9M on July 13, 2026 under a 10b5-1 plan.

ly8.evidence: It is followed by about 47 analysts and owned 87% by institutions.

fi2.evidence: It went from infrastructure monitoring to 24 products and launched Bits AI SRE, LLM Observability and Bits Code/Chat/Agent Builder in 2026.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $1,548M in 2025 (45% of revenue) has produced new product lines that 55% of customers use four or more of.

fi4.evidence: Its land-and-expand model drove about 120% net revenue retention and 4,720 customers above $100K ARR by June 2026, up 23% in a year.

longterm.evidence: Management keeps GAAP operating margin near zero by reinvesting heavily in R&D and new products rather than maximising near-term profit.

gr1.evidence: It has a market value of about $100.6B and trailing revenue of about $3.97B, though it has been public only since 2019.

ni10.evidence: It reported net losses in 2020 ($-24.5M), 2021 ($-20.7M) and 2022 ($-50.2M).

gr4.evidence: Datadog has never paid a dividend.

gr6.evidence: At $280.24 the price is roughly 900 times the 2023-2025 average diluted EPS of about $0.32.

gr7.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 571 times a P/B of about 23 is far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its unified platform and 1,000+ integrations are a clear advantage and it is a five-time Gartner Leader, but rivals such as Dynatrace and Grafana offer comparable core features.

timing.evidence: Cloud migration and AI applications are driving demand, and revenue growth accelerated from 28% in 2025 to 36% in Q2 2026.
